questions.stem: Peter, 42, has 2 days of painless bright red blood on the toilet paper. Partway through your history he asks: "Could this be bowel cancer? My dad died of cancer." You have established that his father died of testicular cancer at 56 and that no one in the family has had bowel cancer or polyps. What is the best response?
options: Reassure him it is almost certainly haemorrhoids, so no further tests will be needed
Tell him his father's cancer puts him at high risk, so he needs urgent screening
Acknowledge his worry, say his dad's cancer doesn't raise his risk, and explain the checks
Offer a home iFOBT kit today so he knows quickly whether a cancer is present
questions.why: Address the worry honestly: testicular cancer in a father does not raise his colorectal cancer risk. But new rectal bleeding still needs examination and colonoscopy, so explain the plan instead of offering blanket reassurance.
notes: This is false reassurance: haemorrhoids found on proctoscopy don't clear the bowel above, and an adult with new rectal bleeding should still have a colonoscopy.
Testicular cancer is not linked to colorectal cancer risk, so this is wrong and needlessly alarming.
The iFOBT is a screening test for people without symptoms; he already has visible bleeding, and a negative result would not exclude cancer.

questions.stem: Peter, 42, has had about 4 days of painless bright red blood on the paper. Proctoscopy shows grade I internal haemorrhoids with fresh blood at 3 o'clock and normal lower rectal mucosa. Hb 151 g/L, ferritin 142 µg/L, CRP 2 mg/L. No change in bowel habit, no weight loss and no family history of bowel cancer. Alongside fibre, fluids and psyllium, what investigation should the GP arrange?
options: Colonoscopy referral to gastroenterology or colorectal surgery
iFOBT now, with colonoscopy referral only if it is positive
CT abdomen and pelvis with contrast to look for a colonic mass
No further tests unless bleeding persists after 6 months of fibre
questions.why: A proctoscope sees only the anal canal and lower rectum, and finding haemorrhoids does not prove they are the only cause. Adults with new rectal bleeding, including those under 50, should be referred for colonoscopy.
notes: An iFOBT is for screening people without symptoms; with visible bleeding a positive result is expected and a negative one does not exclude a lesion.
CT is not the first-line test for the colonic mucosa; it can miss polyps and small cancers, and it cannot take a biopsy.
Waiting months before investigating new rectal bleeding risks delaying the diagnosis of a polyp or cancer above the reach of the proctoscope.

questions.stem: Peter, 42, has had intermittent constipation for years and eats a low-fibre diet at work. Proctoscopy shows congested internal vascular cushions at 3, 7 and 11 o'clock that bleed but do not prolapse on straining. Which mechanism best explains how his haemorrhoids developed?
options: Portal hypertension opening portosystemic anastomoses in the anal canal
A tear in the anoderm from hard stool, with internal sphincter spasm
Obstruction and infection of anal glands in the intersphincteric space
Straining and hard stool engorging the cushions and stretching their supports
questions.why: Haemorrhoids are normal anal vascular cushions. Straining and hard stool slow venous outflow, engorge the cushions and push them down, which weakens the supporting connective tissue. The congested cushions then bleed and, in later grades, prolapse.
notes: Portal hypertension causes anorectal varices, a different condition, and Peter has no features of liver disease.
This is the mechanism of an anal fissure, which is painful and was not seen on proctoscopy.
This is how a perianal abscess and fistula form, which cause pain, swelling or discharge, not painless bleeding.

questions.stem: Peter's proctoscopy shows bleeding internal haemorrhoids above the dentate line, and his bleeding is painless. By contrast, an anal fissure or thrombosed external haemorrhoid below the dentate line is very painful. Which nerve carries pain sensation from the anal canal below the dentate line?
options: Pelvic splanchnic nerves (S2 to S4 parasympathetic)
Inferior rectal nerve (branch of the pudendal nerve)
Genital branch of the genitofemoral nerve (L1 to L2)
questions.why: Below the dentate line the anoderm has somatic innervation from the inferior rectal branch of the pudendal nerve (S2 to S4), so lesions there hurt. Above it, the supply is visceral and autonomic and does not sense somatic pain, which is why internal haemorrhoids are painless.
notes: Pelvic splanchnic nerves give visceral (autonomic) supply above the dentate line, where sharp somatic pain is not felt.
Sympathetic fibres from the inferior hypogastric plexus supply the rectum and upper anal canal, not the somatically sensitive anoderm.
The genitofemoral nerve supplies the scrotum and upper anterior thigh, not the anal canal.
